4093: In March 1967 you were vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. In the last seat at the meeting table sat Lu Genbao, formerly of the Scarlet Guards. On the day of the renaming you had asked for places for the Scarlet Guards. The answer came back as one sentence. Individual mass representatives from the former Scarlet Guards could be admitted after review. There were five names on the list. That night a big-character poster went up outside the Workers' General Headquarters asking whether Wang Hongwen meant to surrender to the royalists. When Lu Genbao went back to his factory, the people in his own workshop called him a traitor. A month later, more than 40 Scarlet Guards held since Kangping Road were released. Two men were still in Huashan Hospital.
4094: In March 1967 you were vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. Order No. 1 included freedom of association, with half a sentence added at the end, “but must not violate the Six Articles on Public Security.” Lines formed at the district registration offices. A few old workers from the former Scarlet Guards registered too, under a new name. At a Workers' General Headquarters meeting someone pounded the table and said you were reversing the verdict on the royalists. In one week more than 2,000 organizations registered. One in Zhabei had a fine-sounding name and turned out to be a gang that went in for beating, smashing and looting. Master Qian was in the line too. He did not look at you. Beijing never replied.
4095: In August 1967 you were the Workers' General Headquarters leader who had led the attack on Shanghai Diesel. In an air-raid shelter in the northeast corner of the plant, more than 40 people were locked up. You had ordered everyone captured to be locked in there to wait for you to question them, and you never went. The guards questioned them themselves. On the third night the man they carried out was the one who had recognized you at the gate on Kangping Road. His name was Lu Genbao. He had been in the Scarlet Guards, and after Kangping Road he joined no organization at all. That day he had come to Shanghai Diesel to look for his nephew, who was an apprentice there. He later died in Huashan Hospital. His wife stood outside the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee for three days holding his work ID. History went on as before. In 1980, when the Special Court looked into Shanghai Diesel Liansi, Lu Genbao's name was on the third page of the casualty list the prosecutor read out.
4096: After September 1971 you were held in an army barracks and investigated as a Shanghai contact of the Lin Biao group. At the end of March you had gone to Yueyang Road for that dinner with Lin Liguo. He asked how many men the Shanghai militia had and whether they had guns, and you answered each question. After September 13, Xu Jingxian invited you to the Jinjiang Hotel to read documents, and men from the Nanjing Military Region were sitting in the room. You said it was a dinner. They said Wang Weiguo also said it was a dinner. You were held in the barracks until 1982 and sentenced to 14 years, counted from 1971. You came out in 1985 and were resettled in the countryside near Changchun. The villagers called you Old Wang.
4097: In February 1975 the Central Committee told you to go back to Shanghai to help with the work. You lived on Xingguo Road and went back to No. 17 Mill one day a week to do manual labor. In October 1974 in Changsha you had told the Chairman to his face that if Deng Xiaoping went on like this he would be a second Lin Biao. The Chairman looked at you for a long time and said, go back. After that, documents no longer came to you first. On October 6, 1976, three people were arrested at Huairen Hall. The next morning someone came to Xingguo Road and took you away. In 1981 you were still sentenced to life. In court someone asked what you had said in Changsha. You said, I said he was Lin Biao.
4098: On the evening of October 6, 1976, you were seized on the stairs at Diaoyutai and never reached Huairen Hall. While the car waited downstairs for you, you had picked up the phone and asked for Shanghai. You told Wang Xiuzhen something was about to happen in Beijing, and the militia should get ready to fight. On the 9th the militia of several factories came out of the factory gates and set up checkpoints on the Waibaidu Bridge and Yan'an Road. On the afternoon of the 10th, Garrison Command troops moved into the city. Nobody ever knew who fired first. Among the dead were a 19-year-old militiaman, a woman from a food shop walking home from work, and a 21-year-old soldier from Henan. Later Shanghai sentenced twice as many people. Huang Jinhai got 18 years. Every year at Qingming the militiaman's mother went to Longhua.
4099: In the winter of 1979 you died in the infirmary of Qincheng Prison, aged 44. The cause of death was written as heart failure. The special case group wanted you to inform on people in Shanghai. You put the pen down and did not write a single word. You did not eat either. They held you down on the bed and poured liquid food in through your nose. You lost weight fast, and one day in the exercise yard you fell straight to the ground. On October 1, Cui Gendi came with the children and waited a whole morning in the visiting room. She did not get to see you. When the Special Court opened in November 1980, nine people stood in the dock. In the indictment your name was followed by a parenthesis, deceased, no further criminal liability.
4100: In 1982 you were sentenced to 12 years for plotting armed rebellion and held in Tilanqiao. On the night of October 9, 1976, you opened the armory at the No. 17 State Cotton Mill, had bullets pressed into magazines, and handed out the guns. On the 13th word came down not to move. The bullets were taken out one by one, and none was missing. In the investigation, though, the people who had opened the armory were put on a separate list. You were on it, and so was Huang Jinhai. You were released in 1988. Your application to go back to the security section was turned down, and the mill sent you to watch a warehouse. It was piled with dismantled spindles.
4101: In October 1976 you never went to Beijing. You were in Shanghai the whole time. At the Kangping Road meeting on the night of the 12th, you said fight. On the morning of the 13th, “Give us back Jiang Qing” went up on Nanjing Road. Militia held People's Square and the gate of the radio station. In the afternoon Ma Tianshui and the others came back from Beijing and told everyone not to move, but the militia at the radio station had already squared off with Garrison Command men. Nobody ever knew who fired first. Seven people died. There were militiamen, a middle school student passing by, and a soldier. It was over by the morning of the 14th. You got a death sentence with a two-year reprieve. The investigation spread down to district level. Zhu Yongjia got 14 years. He said he had said three days, and he never thought it would take only half a day.
4102: In December 1980 you stood in the dock of the Special Court, and you still got life. Your final statement lasted seven minutes. You set out what happened at Anting and at Shanghai Diesel. On Shanghai Diesel, you said the man who should have protected the detainees was not you. The television broadcast cut away in the third minute. The next day the newspapers kept only one sentence, the one where you admitted guilt. The court clerk's record went into a dossier. On the cover was written, not to be viewed by the subject. In the 2020s a graduate student copied that page in an archive and put it in a footnote of her thesis. At her defense her adviser told her to take it out. She did not take it out.
4103: In December 1978 you were in Qincheng Prison. Through the small window in the door you took a newspaper carrying the Third Plenum communiqué. You had walked the road history took. You went to Beijing in 1972, became Vice Chairman of the Central Committee in 1973, were arrested at Huairen Hall on the evening of October 6, 1976, and were moved to Qincheng in April 1977. The man in charge of you brought the Central Committee's material that set out your “criminal evidence.” You said you would write down what you had taken. Your confession went to a fourth draft. What you had not taken you left out, and the special case group still said your attitude was dishonest. The communiqué said the focus of the whole Party's work must shift, and that the Tiananmen Incident was a revolutionary action. You folded the paper and passed it back out through the small window.

4106: In December 1978 you were on duty in the security section of the No. 17 State Cotton Mill. Two sweet potatoes were roasting on the stove, and the mill loudspeakers were broadcasting the Third Plenum communiqué. You never went to Beijing. Order No. 1 in 1967 included freedom of association. In 1968 Beijing wanted it withdrawn. You did not withdraw it. In September you were sent to the May Seventh Cadre School in Fengxian, and in 1971 you came back to the No. 17 Mill security section. When the militia went on alert in October 1976, the mill's guns were never handed out. Guns and ammunition were stored apart. One key to the armory was in the security section, and the other was with Zhu Guoqiang, the militia company commander. The Expose-Criticize-Investigate campaign made you write materials three times. Every time the questions were about Order No. 1 of 1967. The third time, the young man who came said, Master Wang, your case is really not a big deal.

4112: In December 1978 you were held at Tilanqiao in Shanghai, and your case had not yet been decided. Huang Jinhai was in the next cell block. You never went to Beijing. You stayed in Shanghai. At the Kangping Road meeting on the night of October 12, 1976, Ma Tianshui, Xu Jingxian and Wang Xiuzhen had gone to Beijing and not come back. Zhu Yongjia said fight, and then it was your turn to speak. You said put the guns away. You would go to the Garrison Command, and Lu Genbao should go round the factories and tell the former Scarlet Guards to stay off the streets. That night the Garrison commander kept you sitting there all night. Lu Genbao went to more than 20 factories, and not one former Scarlet Guard went out on the street. On the afternoon of the 13th, Ma Tianshui and the others came back, and Shanghai was quiet. At the end of 1976 you were placed under isolation and investigation. Lu Genbao came to see you at Tilanqiao once. He talked to you through the iron bars and brought a padded jacket.
4113: In December 1978 you were held at Tilanqiao in Shanghai, and your case had not yet been decided. Huang Jinhai was in the next cell block. You never went to Beijing. You stayed in Shanghai. At the Kangping Road meeting on the night of October 12, 1976, Ma Tianshui, Xu Jingxian and Wang Xiuzhen had gone to Beijing and not come back. Zhu Yongjia said fight, and then it was your turn to speak. You said Shanghai's business should be put to a vote of Shanghai's people. Let the voters say whether to fight or not. On the morning of the 13th, more than ten communes in Yangpu District held meetings. The voters sat room after room, and most said do not fight. In the afternoon Ma Tianshui and the others came back and told everyone not to move. At the end of 1976 you were placed under isolation and investigation. The investigation group kept coming back to ask about that vote, and who had given you the idea of a vote. You said, 1967.

4118: In December 1978 you worked in an office at the Ministry of Railways. You had no post, and every day you read documents at the set hours. In 1975 you went to Deng Xiaoping and took a work team to Xuzhou to put the railways in order. The rebel leader in Xuzhou asked you, you're one of us, so why have you come to straighten us out? In 1976, during the campaign to Counterattack the Right-Deviationist Wind, an article called you a capitulationist who had climbed up from among the workers. 4120: In December 1978 you were spending your second winter in the barracks at Maqiao in Shanghai. The investigation had reached no conclusion. 4126: In December 1978 you were under investigation in a compound in the Western Hills of Beijing, where you had been for two years and two months. In autumn 1975 you went to take charge of restoring the All-China Federation of Trade Unions. 4127: In December 1978 you were Vice Chairman of the ACFTU. The chairman was Ni Zhifu. In autumn 1975 you went to take charge of restoring the All-China Federation of Trade Unions. 4139:
On November 13, Zhang Chunqiao signed the five points at Culture Square, and the Workers' General Headquarters became a legal organization. Two or three days later a central meeting was held in Beijing. Mao Zedong took out the Constitution at the meeting and read the passage on freedom of association. He asked whether workers had freedom of association. He also said that on the Shanghai question Zhang Chunqiao was right. First the facts, then the policy. When these words got back to Shanghai, the Municipal Party Committee could no longer call the WGHQ illegal.

By now the few hundred who would not come back had walked as far as Suzhou. On the 14th Huang Jinhai went after them to talk them round, and Geng Jinzhang locked him in a bathhouse. That evening Geng Jinzhang negotiated with Zhang Chunqiao and raised another Five Demands. Zhang Chunqiao signed. Han Zheyi, secretary of the East China Bureau, and Cao Diqiu signed too. On the 18th the Municipal Party Committee sent vehicles to bring these 400-odd people back to Shanghai. They got off outside the Hongdu Theater. As they got off, Geng Jinzhang insisted that everyone leave their details for a contact list.

The Municipal Party Committee was moving too. On the 19th Cao Diqiu received a group of representatives of conservative workers. On the 20th the Municipal Party Committee issued a notice strictly banning setting up private courts and arresting, kidnapping or beating people on one's own authority. On the 23rd these representatives held a preparatory meeting in the conference room of the Yangpu District Party Committee and took the name Shanghai Workers' Scarlet Guards Headquarters. Cao Diqiu said the Municipal Party Committee supported them. The WGHQ had a signature from someone in the Central Cultural Revolution Group. The Scarlet Guards had the Municipal Party Committee behind them. From then on the workers of Shanghai were split into two sides.
4140:
History At a central meeting Mao Zedong took out the Constitution and read the passage on “freedom of association,” and said that on the Shanghai question Zhang Chunqiao was right, first the facts, then the policy. Wang Li, The First Year of the “Cultural Revolution” (《“文革”第一年》), quoted in Wang Rui, “Rethinking and Re-examining the ‘Anting Incident’” (paraphrased).

Disputed The date of the meeting. Wang Rui, drawing on the various accounts, gives November 16. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), records a Politburo meeting on November 15. Here it is written as “two or three days later.”

History On November 14 Huang Jinhai went after them to Suzhou and was held by Geng Jinzhang in a bathhouse. That evening Geng Jinzhang negotiated with Zhang Chunqiao and raised another Five Demands, and Zhang Chunqiao, Han Zheyi and Cao Diqiu all signed. On the 18th the Municipal Party Committee sent vehicles to bring them back. When they got off at the Hongdu Theater, Geng Jinzhang insisted on keeping a contact list. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 4.

History On November 19 Cao Diqiu received representatives of conservative workers. On the 23rd they held a preparatory meeting in the conference room of the Yangpu District Party Committee and took the name “Shanghai Workers' Scarlet Guards Headquarters.” Cao Diqiu said the Municipal Party Committee supported them. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), chs. 4 and 5. The Municipal Party Committee's notice of November 20 banning setting up private courts and arresting, kidnapping or beating people on one's own authority appears in Article 6 of the Scarlet Guards' Eight Demands as recorded in Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 13 (paraphrased).
4141: The Municipal Party Committee Gives Way
4142:
After Kangping Road the Municipal Party Committee had lost both sides. On December 25 Cao Diqiu declared his signature void. The Scarlet Guards felt the committee had dropped them, and they soon turned around and denounced it for surrendering to the rebels. The rebels had always meant to bring the committee down.

The city stopped too. From early on the 30th the railways stopped running and the post and telegraph offices closed. Scarlet Guards left the factories in large numbers. Some went north to petition, and some went to escape struggle sessions. The No. 17 State Cotton Mill alone lost more than 2,900 people, and in the workshops the machines stopped one after another. Zhou Enlai ordered that transport must not be cut. He also ordered the arrest of Wang Yuxi, a Scarlet Guards leader who had taken trains without authority to send people to Beijing.

On the evening of New Year's Day 1967, Cao Diqiu held a cadre meeting on Xiangshan Road and passed on Chen Pixian's words. On economic questions, loosen up a bit, don't resist. The meeting set five points. Long-term temporary workers and outsourced workers could be made permanent workers, and workers sent down to support agriculture after 1958 could go back to their old factories. Once word of this went out, people came to the door wanting back pay, wanting to be made permanent, wanting to return to the city. Some units paid out several months' money at once. Long lines formed outside the banks, and some banks had runs.

By January 3 the Municipal Party Committee was still there, but the rebels did not listen to what it said, and the Scarlet Guards no longer believed it.
4143:
History On December 25 Cao Diqiu declared the signature void. The Scarlet Guards then turned to accusing the Municipal Party Committee of surrendering to the rebels. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5; Meisner, Mao's China and After.

History From December 30 the railways stopped and the post and telegraph offices closed, and large numbers of Scarlet Guards left their factories. Zhou Enlai ordered that transport not be cut and ordered the arrest of Wang Yuxi, who had taken trains without authority. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5. The figure of more than 2,900 people leaving the No. 17 State Cotton Mill is from Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 13 (paraphrased).

Disputed The cause of the stoppage. Huang Jinhai says someone at Scarlet Guards headquarters proposed the “Three Stoppages” and it was partly carried out. Li Xun holds that headquarters never decided on the Three Stoppages, and that the actual stoppage came from large numbers of Scarlet Guards leaving their factories to go north or to avoid struggle sessions. See the same two books.

History On the evening of January 1, 1967, Cao Diqiu chaired a cadre meeting on Xiangshan Road and passed on Chen Pixian's “on economic questions, loosen up a bit, don't resist.” Five points were set. Among them, long-term temporary workers and outsourced workers could become permanent workers, and workers sent down to support agriculture after 1958 could go back to their old factories. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 6. Demands for back pay, permanent status and return to the city then poured in, some units paid out money freely, and some banks had runs. Yang Jisheng, The World Turned Upside Down (《天地翻覆》), ch. 11; Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), chs. 16 and 17 (paraphrased).
4146:
After the four central bodies sent their congratulatory telegram on January 11, every rebel organization headed into the government offices. A single bureau often had two or three groups arrive one after another to take it over. The later arrivals said the earlier ones were grabbing power, and the earlier ones said the later ones had a mountaintop mentality. Several hundred organizations each held a few official seals, and none would give way to another.

In mid-January the Workers' General Headquarters moved its headquarters into the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions building on the Bund. In November, when the Scarlet Guards were being set up, the federation had given them Room 103 in that building as an office. Historically, Wang Hongwen was not very keen on fighting over offices. When people brought him seals, he had them locked up in the No. 17 Mill security section.

Production fell to Ma Tianshui. On January 6 he had still been on the stage at a struggle session alongside Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu. Later Zhang Chunqiao won him over, and he came across. From then on he ran production at the ports, the power plants and the factories. There was now someone to run production. Who would be in charge above that was still unsettled.
4147:
History In January rebel organizations everywhere fought over government offices and accused each other of “grabbing power” and a “mountaintop mentality.” This is where the later “great alliance” came from. Source to be added (based on a summary in the original source notes for Act Two of the game).

History The Workers' General Headquarters moved to the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions building on the Bund in mid-January 1967. When the Scarlet Guards were being set up in November 1966, the federation gave them Room 103 as an office. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), chs. 4 and 5.

History Wang Hongwen was not keen on the scramble for offices. When people brought him seals, he had them locked up in the No. 17 Mill security section. Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), chs. 17 and 18 (paraphrased).

History Ma Tianshui was denounced at a struggle session together with Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu on January 6. Afterward, persuaded by Zhang Chunqiao, he “came across,” and for a long time after he ran Shanghai's industrial production. Wikipedia, “Ma Tianshui”; NetEase and others (search summary).
4149:
The 400-odd people who came back from Suzhou were the core of the Second Regiment. Its full name was the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters Second Regiment of Workers Returning to Shanghai from the North. On paper it came under the Workers' General Headquarters, but Geng Jinzhang did not listen much to headquarters. Geng Jinzhang's original name was Geng Yuzhang. He was from Shandong. Captured from the Nationalist army in the Battle of Jinan, he joined the People's Liberation Army at once and rose to deputy platoon leader. He joined the Party in 1949, was demobilized to Shanghai in 1957, and worked at a paper mill as a beater operator.

The Second Regiment kept pulling in more people. By early 1967 it claimed 500,000 to 600,000 members, and for a time it was bigger than the WGHQ itself. Huang Jinhai later said Zhang Chunqiao deliberately propped up the Second Regiment to hold the WGHQ in check. On the night of Kangping Road, Geng Jinzhang got a call from Zhang Chunqiao's secretary, hurried back from Beijing and set up a command post. The scene inside the compound belonged to the Second Regiment. When the Scarlet Guards went north, Second Regiment men were among those who went to Kunshan to stop them. On the “Urgent Notice” in January, Geng Jinzhang got in first and signed in the name of the WGHQ. Headquarters later had Fan Zuodong sign it again.

At the end of January, as the new government was being prepared, more than 600 organizations all wanted a recognized place in it, and the quarrel went on for days. On the night of February 4, Zhang Chunqiao renamed the 38 member units as founding units, with no announcement in the papers and no names signed. Only then did things quiet down. The Second Regiment was large, and Geng Jinzhang never accepted the place he was given in the lineup.
4150:
History Geng Jinzhang, originally named Geng Yuzhang, was from Shandong and a private first class in the Nationalist army. Captured in the Battle of Jinan, he joined the People's Liberation Army and rose to deputy platoon leader. He joined the Party in 1949 and was demobilized in 1957 to a Shanghai paper mill, where he worked as a beater operator. ifeng.com, “Geng Jinzhang, Wang Hongwen's ‘Sworn Enemy,’ Remembers,” and others (search summary).

History On the return from Suzhou, Geng Jinzhang insisted on keeping a contact list, and with these 400-odd people as a base he built the “Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters Second Regiment of Workers Returning to Shanghai from the North.” Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 4.

Disputed Whether the Second Regiment's core came from the people who went to Suzhou. Other sources do not say so. The figure of “500,000 to 600,000” is the Second Regiment's own claim. That Zhang Chunqiao propped up the Second Regiment to hold the Workers' General Headquarters in check is Huang Jinhai's view.

Disputed The scene at Kangping Road. Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 14, citing Dai Liqing's recollections, says the scene belonged to the Second Regiment. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5, says WGHQ headquarters sent no one, and those present were the “Red Guard Army” and the Second Regiment. On Geng Jinzhang getting a call from Zhang Chunqiao's secretary on the 29th and hurrying back from Beijing to set up a command post, see Wikipedia, “Kangping Road Incident,” and RFA, “The Battle of Kangping Road” (search summary).

Disputed Who went to Kunshan to stop people. Huang Jinhai says WGHQ headquarters sent no one, and those who went were Red Guards and the Second Regiment. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5.

History Geng Jinzhang first signed the “Urgent Notice” in the name of the WGHQ, and Fan Zuodong later signed it in his place. Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 6. On the night of February 4, Zhang Chunqiao renamed the 38 member units as founding units, with no announcement in the papers and no names signed, to settle the fight among more than 600 organizations over recognition. Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 20 (paraphrased).

Fiction Geng Jinzhang “never accepting” his place is the game's summary. It is based on the Second Regiment's discontent with the makeup of the commune and its plan to make trouble at the founding rally (Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 7).
4153:
After that day at Shanghai Diesel, the two factions in other provinces were still fighting. In August the two factions in Nanjing fought hard. The Nanjing Military Region backed the August 27 faction, Zhang Chunqiao backed the Red General Headquarters, and Xu Shiyou hid in the Dabie Mountains. In September the Chairman had Zhang Chunqiao bring Xu Shiyou to Shanghai to see him. On his southern tour the Chairman said there was no fundamental conflict of interest within the working class, and still less any reason for it to split into two irreconcilable factions. This was printed in the papers.

On August 4 the Chairman wrote to Jiang Qing that more than 75 percent of army cadres supported the Right, and the Left should be armed. After that both factions everywhere were given guns. The Chairman later told foreign visitors that a million guns had been handed out in all. The Shanghai militia was built starting from that night.

In May 1968 the Chairman approved and circulated the experience of the military control committee at the Beijing Xinhua Printing Plant in struggle against the enemy. From then on the Cleansing the Class Ranks campaign spread across the whole country. It looked into everyone's history.
4154:
History On the two factions in Nanjing, Xu Shiyou hiding in the Dabie Mountains, Mao Zedong having Zhang Chunqiao invite Xu Shiyou to Shanghai, and the remarks on the September southern tour, see Yang Jisheng, The World Turned Upside Down (《天地翻覆》), ch. 15 (paraphrased).

History On Mao Zedong's August 4 letter to Jiang Qing about arming the Left, his telling foreign visitors that a million guns were handed out, and the Shanghai militia starting from that night, see ibid., ch. 15 (paraphrased), and the background panel for “A Stick” in Act Three.

History On Mao Zedong approving and circulating the Xinhua Printing Plant experience in May 1968 and Cleansing the Class Ranks spreading across the country, see ibid., ch. 19 (paraphrased).
4156:
The two factions in Guangxi, one called Alliance Command and the other April 22, kept fighting and would not sit down together. The Central Committee held a study class in Beijing for the leaders of both factions.

On July 3 the Central Committee, the State Council, the Central Military Commission and the Central Cultural Revolution Group jointly issued a proclamation. It said that in some places in Guangxi people were sabotaging rail traffic, looting aid supplies bound for Vietnam and attacking army units, and this must be firmly stopped.

That summer many people died in Guangxi. Most of the dead were from the April 22 faction, and very few were from Alliance Command. Those killed in armed fighting were only a small share. Most were beaten to death or shot in organized killings, and the organizers were mostly grassroots authorities at county level and below. Yang Jisheng divides the mass killings of the Cultural Revolution into three peaks. The third was the suppression in 1968, by military and government groups, of mass organizations that opposed the revolutionary committees.
4157:
History On the study class the Central Committee held in Beijing in 1968 for the two Guangxi factions, and the proclamation issued jointly by the four bodies on July 3, see Yang Jisheng, The World Turned Upside Down (《天地翻覆》), ch. 19 (paraphrased), and the background panel for “Study Class” in Act Three.

History Most of the 1968 dead in Guangxi were on the April 22 side. Most were beaten to death or shot in organized killings, and those who directly organized them were mostly grassroots authorities at county level and below. On this and on the three peaks of mass killing, see ibid., ch. 19 (paraphrased).
4159:
The Party Constitution of the Ninth Party Congress said Lin Biao was the Chairman's successor. After his plane came down in Mongolia on September 13, 1971, that passage was void. Nobody said aloud who would take over.

That year the people who had risen through rebellion were on their way down. The more than two million troops sent out to the localities to support the left during the Cultural Revolution were withdrawn in stages from 1972. By 1972, nearly half the mass representatives in the leadership of Shanghai's industrial, financial and trade units had been purged.

Historically, Wang Hongwen became a Central Committee member at the Ninth Party Congress in 1969. Before he went up to speak, he borrowed 15 yuan from Xu Jingxian and bought a pair of black Dacron trousers. In January 1971 he was elected secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee, third in rank, and he still drew his wages from No. 17 Mill. There is no reliable direct record of why the Chairman picked him. The common view is that the Chairman wanted to train a successor from among young workers who had risen through rebellion.
